summary_plain: This investigation burns methane and ethylene diffusion flames in the microgravity environment of the International Space Station. Researchers study how flame shape, temperatures, soot formation, and extinction limits change under different fuel dilutions and velocities. Understanding these behaviors helps improve computational models and fire safety designs for spacecraft.
summary_expert: The ACME CLD Flame investigation studies coflow laminar diffusion flames of methane and ethylene in microgravity to provide benchmark data for testing computational models at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum. The research varies velocity and fuel dilution to characterize weak coflow diffusion flames and sooting tendencies in long-residence-time flames. Planned and executed measurements include flame shape, lift-off heights, gas temperatures, soot luminosity, soot temperatures, and soot volume fractions using diagnostics such as chemiluminescence, thin-filament pyrometry, and laser extinction. The provided documents describe the objectives, approach, and design only.

key_findings.text: The investigation planned to characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, lift-off heights, temperatures and extinction limits.

The project aimed to characterize the sooting tendencies of diffusion flames with long residence times, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, by measuring flame shape, gas temperatures in the soot-free portion of the flame, soot luminosity, soot temperatures, and soot volume fractions.
Researchers planned to study methane and ethylene diffusion flames over a wide range of test conditions to generate improved computational models with advanced soot sub-models.
